5	Question Does prenatal and infancy homevisitation by nurses reduce obesity and hypertension among mothers with very low income and their first-born offspring at 12 and 18 years following birth?
6	
7	Findings In this randomized clinical trial of 742 participants, nurse-visited female offspring had lower rates of obesity and severe obesity at age 12 and 18 years combined than their control group counterparts; nurse-visited mothers of females had lower rates of stage 1 and stage 2 hypertension at child age 12 and 18 years combined compared with their control group counterparts. No intervention effect was found for these outcomes among male offspring or mothers of males.
8	
9	Meaning These findings suggest that prenatal and infancy home visitation holds promise for reducing obesity among female offspring living in extreme poverty and reducing their mothers' hypertension.

36	
37	Poverty and adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) pose substantial risks for a range of health problems, 1-4 including obesity among female children and adolescents 5 and hypertensive disorders among adults. 6-10 These disparities are especially pronounced among females and Black individuals. 11-13 Obesity and hypertension are major public health concerns because they increase the risk for a variety of chronic health conditions, including cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and kidney failure, as well as premature mortality. 11,14,15 Addressing these conditions among people living with very low income, and especially among Black individuals, is a public health imperative. 16
38	
39	The Nurse-Family Partnership (NFP) is a program of prenatal and infant and toddler home visiting by nurses designed to improve outcomes of (1) pregnancy, (2) child health and development, and (3) maternal health and life course (eMethods in Supplement 2). 17,18 The NFP has been tested in a series of randomized clinical trials in the US for different populations living in different contexts, with replicated benefits found in these domains in at least 2 of these trials. 17,18 Many program effects were most pronounced among families experiencing the greatest adversity. 18 The focus of the current investigation is on participants in Memphis, Tennessee, living in deep poverty and in resource-poor neighborhoods. 19 Program effects on maternal and child health in this trial have been reported for prenatal health (including pregnancy-induced hypertension), 19 child health and development, 19-23 and maternal health and life course. 19-21,24-26

findings.location: Results, first demographic paragraph (page 5): maternal ethnicity at child age 18 y
findings.quote: One mother (0.2%) reported Hispanic ethnicity, and 617 mothers (98.8%) reported non-Hispanic ethnicity.
findings.reproduction_problem: The primary tool used was grim_percentage, which is MCP-only and has no CLI verb; the grim-sweep command shown reproduces the identical arithmetic (an empty n-set at n=618 is the same failure).
findings.notes: With n=618 stated in the same sentence, no integer count yields 98.8%: 610/618 = 98.7% and 611/618 = 98.9%. The percentage is also inconsistent with its own numerator, since 617 of 618 is 99.8%. Both the denominator (618) and the [0,100] bound on percentages are stated/logically necessary, not assumed, so the impossibility does not rest on any inferred constraint. The most economical explanation is a transposition of 99.8 to 98.8 rather than a data-integrity problem, but it is an arithmetic impossibility as printed.

findings.location: Results, first demographic paragraph (page 5): maternal ethnicity at child age 18 y

findings.notes: Hispanic and non-Hispanic are an exhaustive two-category split of the 618 mothers, so the two percentages must sum to 100 within rounding (+/-0.1). They sum to 99.0, a shortfall of 1.0 percentage point. Independent corroboration of the GRIM-percentage failure on the same figure.

findings.reproduction_problem: grim_percentage is MCP-only (no CLI verb); the grim-sweep form shown reproduces the same arithmetic for the n=594 leg. The contrasting n=618 leg requires a second run with --n-min 618 --n-max 618.
findings.notes: The paragraph describes the 594 mothers interviewed at child age 12 y, then asserts 'All 618 reported non-Hispanic ethnicity'. GRIM confirms the denominator for this block is 594 (559/594 = 94.1%, and 3/594 + 559/594 + 32/594 sum exactly to 594 and to 100.0%), while 94.1% is unattainable at n=618. 618 is the child-age-18 interview total, so a figure from the wrong follow-up wave has been inserted into the 12-year sentence. A cross-reference error, not a data anomaly.

findings.quote: ARR(95%CI)b Pvaluec -- Two-sided asymptotic P value for the null hypothesis that the treatment effect is 0.

inputs.method: SE recovered from CI width on the log scale, p recovered by normal approximation

computed.null_rows_direction: mixed and small in both directions
computed.eTable_LSMD_estimates_direction: reconcile essentially exactly (191.37 g, -2.226, -4.064, -0.553 all consistent)

findings.notes: This is the paper's central statistical inconsistency and it is systematic, not sporadic. Every one of the 17 ARR rows the paper declares significant has a reported p-value SMALLER than the p implied by its own printed 95% CI, most by a factor of 2-5 and one by more than 17. Among non-significant rows the discrepancies are small and run in both directions, and the continuous LSMD estimates quoted from eTables 5-6 reconcile almost exactly -- so this is not a global rounding or tooling artifact but is confined to the ARR rows carrying the paper's claims. A benign explanation exists and should be stated: the CI may be a delta-method or bootstrap interval on the relative-risk scale while the p-value comes from a Wald test on the underlying logistic coefficient, and post-double-selection lasso inference can produce differing variance estimates. The paper does not say this, and as printed a reader cannot reproduce any reported p from its own interval. Directionality is what elevates this above bookkeeping: a variance-estimator mismatch has no reason to be one-signed across every significant row.

findings.location: Abstract RESULTS; Results, Obesity section; Table 1, Severe obesity at age 12 and 18 y, Female
findings.quote: and severe obesity (ARR, 0.185; 95% CI, 0.046-0.748; P<.001)
findings.notes: The single largest p/CI divergence in the paper, and it sits in the Abstract, the Key Points and the Conclusions. The point estimate is properly log-centred within its interval (implied centre 0.1855 vs 0.185 printed), so the CI is internally coherent -- but that same interval yields z = -2.37, p = 0.018, more than an order of magnitude above the claimed P<.001. Under the paper's own Romano-Wolf correction this row carries MHT P = .04, which is far closer to the CI-implied 0.018 than the raw P<.001 is, so the corrected column is not consistent with the uncorrected one either. This is the headline finding for the 81% severe-obesity reduction in female offspring. Note also that the effect rests on very few events: at the trial's 514:228 allocation the treatment arm of this row holds roughly 80 girls at a reported proportion of 0.02, i.e. about 2 cases.

findings.location: Abstract RESULTS; Results, Hypertension section; Table 4, Maternal stage 2 hypertension at age 12 and 18 y, Mothers of females

findings.reproduction_problem: The batch form debit_check_batch is MCP-only; the single-row CLI command shown reproduces the decisive sensitivity case (n=80 returns consistent, refuting the n=269 impossible verdict).
findings.notes: This is a negative result that had to be actively guarded. The four main tables report every outcome as a binary 0/1 proportion with an SD, which is the textbook DEBIT target -- but the ns printed are ROW totals spanning both arms, while the proportions are per-arm, and per-arm sample sizes appear nowhere in the paper. Running DEBIT with the row total produced three 'impossible' verdicts; sweeping plausible arm sizes flips every one of them to consistent. Those three verdicts are artifacts of the substituted n and are NOT reported as findings. The correct conclusion is that the missing per-arm denominators block DEBIT, GRIM and SPRITE across all 138 proportion cells -- a reporting gap that removes the paper's most checkable surface from scrutiny.

findings.notes: No evidence of copy-paste or recycled data. Every repeated (mean, SD) pair the tool surfaced lies between blocks that describe the SAME participants (Tables 1 and 3 are both the offspring cohort; Tables 2 and 4 are both the mothers), which I declared via sample_id, so none is an independent-source match. findings.notes: A multiplicity-corrected p-value that is smaller than its uncorrected counterpart is not strictly impossible under Romano-Wolf, because the stepdown p is read off a bootstrap null distribution rather than obtained by inflating the asymptotic p. The row that warrants clarification regardless is Table 4 stage 1 at age 12 y, mothers of females, where the MHT column prints '.00' against a raw '.01'. computed.verdict: equivalence cannot be assessed; no conclusion of no effect is licensed

findings.notes: The tool declines to judge without a stated smallest effect size of interest, and that refusal IS the result: the paper specifies no SESOI and performs no equivalence test, so 'no intervention effect' is not supported by these intervals. The male offspring intervals are strikingly wide -- severe obesity at 12 and 18 y in males remains compatible with a 3.75-fold INCREASE in risk, and stage 1 hypertension in males with a 4.55-fold effect in either direction. Three male obesity rows in fact point toward higher risk in the nurse-visited arm (ARRs 1.454, 1.510, 1.517). The maternal rows are the exception: Table 2's intervals are genuinely narrow (e.g. 0.839-1.234), so 'no effect' is far better supported for mothers' obesity than for male offspring. The abstract's single undifferentiated null claim papers over that difference, and the paper leans on it in the Discussion to explain the sex moderation.

findings.location: Table 1 (severe obesity 12 and 18 y, female) and Table 4 (stage 2 hypertension 12 and 18 y, mothers of females)
findings.quote: a mean (SD) proportion of 0.57 (0.50) had stage 1 hypertension and 0.27 (0.44) had stage 2 hypertension
findings.notes: Recorded as a deliberate negative check on the most tempting narrative. Relative risks of 0.185 and 0.217 sound extraordinary for a home-visiting programme measured 12-18 years after it ended, but on the standardized scale they are g = 0.35 and g = 0.56 -- one at the medicine_rct median, the other just past the 75th percentile and well inside the usual range. The apparent drama comes from ratios computed on low base rates, not from an implausibly large effect. findings.notes: This is the paper's central statistical inconsistency and it is systematic rather than sporadic. Every one of the 17 ARR rows the paper declares significant has a reported p-value SMALLER than the p implied by its own printed 95% CI, most by a factor of 2 to 5 and one by more than 17. Among non-significant rows the discrepancies are small and run in both directions, and the continuous LSMD estimates quoted from eTables 5 and 6 reconcile almost exactly, so this is not a global rounding or tooling artifact but is confined to the ARR rows carrying the paper's claims. A benign explanation exists and should be stated: the CI may be a delta-method or bootstrap interval on the relative-risk scale while the p-value comes from a Wald test on the underlying logistic coefficient, and post-double-selection lasso inference can produce differing variance estimates. The paper does not say this, and as printed a reader cannot reproduce any reported p from its own interval.
